translation_principles.philosophical_grounding: Benjamin's 'Task of the Translator' — finding the intended effect upon the target language that produces in it the echo of the original. The untranslatable is the only element that will make it across.
translation_principles.fidelity_measure: Not literalism but the survival of the poetic. The worst betrayal is taking a poem that in its source language is excellent and rendering it stilted, mediocre, and unexceptional in the target language.
translation_principles.sources_and_numbering: Sappho follows Lobel-Page (1955) and Voigt (1971). Catullus follows standard numbering. Other poets cited by standard fragment numbers from their respective critical editions. Ellipses and gaps reflect lacunae in the original papyri and manuscripts; some fragments expanded for poetic effect while preserving the sense of incompleteness.

sky_position_hint.constitutional_role_in_sky: The Sappho Room itself, made visible. The bright central star is Sappho 31; the surrounding constellation is the rest of the translations, organized by movement (First Rays → Bright Morning → Zenith → Fading Light → Middle Night). The constellation forms a five-arc arrangement around the Sappho 31 star.
sky_position_hint.companion_star: Catullus 51 — placed immediately after Sappho 31 in the collection; bound to it by the σ_S → σ_C lossy compression
constellation_other_canonical_works: Sappho 1 (Hymn to Aphrodite) — the most complete surviving Sapphic poem, anchor of the Zenith movement
Sappho 44 (Hector and Andromache) — the wedding song of the Zenith
Sappho 58 (The Tithonus Poem) — anchor of Middle Night, on age
Catullus 101 (At His Brother's Grave) — closing companion in Middle Night
